911.title: Bodhidharma
911.hook: the legendary Indian monk Chan remembers at its beginning, sitting with his face to a wall
911.howItsDone: In Soto Zen meditation halls in Japan, practitioners sit facing the wall, and Chan and Zen temples honor Bodhidharma's image as the first ancestor.

segments.voice: Yesterday, four Chinese schools: Tiantai, Huayan, Chan and Pure Land. Your line: four Chinese schools. Could you name all four without looking? Today we step into one of them, Chan, at the place it says it began. Day nine hundred eleven.

A blank wall. Rough plaster, a crack running down one corner. In front of it, a monk sits with his back to the room. Visitors come and go behind him. He doesn't turn around. In paintings he's drawn with a thick beard, heavy brows and wide, unblinking eyes. In Japan he became a round red doll with no arms or legs, weighted at the bottom, so that every time you knock it over it rocks back upright. This is Bodhidharma, the monk Chan remembers at its beginning in China.
screen: `A MONK FACING A WALL.` → `BEARD, BROWS, WIDE EYES.` → `A DOLL THAT ROCKS BACK UP.`

segments.voice: First, who he was, as far as anyone can say. Tradition says he was a monk from India, some accounts say from the south and from a royal family, who came to China to teach. Beyond that, little about him is certain, and the stories about him grew longer and more colorful in the retelling. So it's honest to call him legendary: a real memory, wrapped in a great deal of story. Second, facing the wall. The Chan stories say he settled at a monastery on Mount Song and sat facing a wall, for years, saying little. A short teaching attributed to him speaks of wall-gazing: settling the mind so it stands like a wall, unmoved, with no difference left between self and other. Whether the wall was a real wall, a picture of the mind, or both, the image stuck. Third, the first ancestor. Chan tells its history as a line of teachers handing the teaching to students, mind to mind. In that line, Bodhidharma is counted as the first ancestor in China, the link back to India. Over the next few days we'll meet the emperor who didn't understand him and the student who did. Fourth, why a wall. A wall gives you nothing. No view, no story, nothing to scroll. What's left is whatever the mind brings. That's the point. The red doll in Japan carries the same idea in a lighter key: knocked over, it comes back up, the way attention comes back after it wanders.
screen: `A MONK FROM INDIA, MOSTLY LEGEND.` · `WALL-GAZING ON MOUNT SONG.` · `CHAN'S FIRST ANCESTOR IN CHINA.` · `A WALL GIVES YOU NOTHING.` · then, large: `FACING THE WALL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit facing a wall for two minutes. If you can, turn your chair or your body toward a plain wall, close enough to see it but not so close you strain. Let your eyes rest, half open, on one spot. Nothing to look at, nothing to fix. When a thought appears, let it play against the wall like a shadow, and let it pass. When you notice you've drifted, come back, like the doll rocking upright. If you can't face a wall, lower your gaze to the floor. The bell holds the time.
Bodhidharma. The legendary monk from India whom Chan counts as its first ancestor in China, remembered sitting with his face to a wall. Today's word.
Your line: facing the wall. Today, when you're waiting somewhere, skip the screen for one minute and look at a plain surface instead. Day nine hundred eleven.

912.title: No merit
912.hook: an emperor lists his temples and asks what merit he has made; Bodhidharma says none
912.howItsDone: Making merit through giving and service is part of Buddhist life in many forms, and some Chan and Zen teachers retell the Emperor Wu story as a warning against keeping score.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bodhidharma, the legendary monk with his face to the wall. Your line: facing the wall. What showed up when there was nothing to look at? Day nine hundred twelve.

Temples built. Sutras copied. Monks and nuns supported. Offerings given. That's the list an emperor brings, in the old Chan story, to the strange monk from India. The emperor is Wu of Liang, a ruler devoted to Buddhism, and he wants to know one thing: after all this, how much merit have I made? It's a fair question. It's the kind of question a person asks after years of doing good. And Bodhidharma's answer is short. No merit. Today, what he might have meant.

First, the emperor's list. Merit, in Buddhist teaching, is the good that comes from good actions, and Buddhist texts speak of making it by giving, by supporting monks and by building places to practice. The emperor was doing exactly that. So the answer stings. Second, how the Platform Sutra explains it. In that text a local official, puzzled by the story, asks the teacher Huineng what Bodhidharma meant. Huineng says the emperor's building and giving bring blessings, good fortune, and that's real. But merit in the deeper sense, he says, is something else: it's seeing your own true nature, and treating everyone with the same humble respect. It isn't stored up like grain in a barn. It's found inside, in how you see and how you act. Third, another telling. The Blue Cliff Record, a later book of Chan stories, opens with a different version of the meeting. There the emperor asks, what is the highest meaning of the holy truths? Bodhidharma answers: vast emptiness, nothing holy. The emperor asks, then who is standing in front of me? Bodhidharma says: I don't know. The emperor doesn't understand, and Bodhidharma leaves and crosses the river north. Fourth, what the story aims at. It doesn't say giving is foolish; Huineng says it brings blessings. It aims at the ledger, the quiet counting in the back of the mind. A kindness done while keeping score is still a kindness. The Chan question is what it would feel like to do it with no scoreboard running at all.
screen: `THE EMPEROR'S LIST.` · `BLESSINGS ARE NOT MERIT.` · `VAST EMPTINESS, NOTHING HOLY.` · `GIVING WITHOUT A LEDGER.` · then, large: `NO MERIT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do good without counting. Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Bring to mind something kind you did recently, small or large. Notice whether a little scoreboard lights up somewhere: that was good of me, I'll remember that, they owe me one. Don't scold it. Just see it, and let the number fade. Then choose one small good thing you could do today that no one will ever know was you. Hold it lightly, and come back to the breath. The bell holds the time.
No merit. Bodhidharma's short answer to an emperor's list, aimed not at giving but at the counting. Today's word.
Your line: no merit. Today, do one good thing that no one will know was you, and don't tell anyone. Day nine hundred twelve.

913.title: Bring me your mind
913.hook: Huike asks Bodhidharma to put his mind at peace; Bodhidharma says, bring it here
913.howItsDone: Chan and Zen students study the exchange between Bodhidharma and Huike as a koan, and meditation teachers in several traditions invite students to turn and look directly at the mind that worries.

segments.voice: Yesterday, an emperor's list of good deeds, and Bodhidharma's answer. Your line: no merit. Did you manage one kindness with no scoreboard running? Day nine hundred thirteen.

Snow is falling. A man stands outside a monastery, waiting. Inside, the monk he has come to see sits facing a wall and doesn't turn around. The man is Huike. He has come a long way with one trouble, the kind that follows a person from room to room. When at last he speaks, he doesn't ask a clever question. He says: my mind isn't at peace. Please, teacher, settle it for me. Today, the answer he got.
screen: `SNOW, AND A MAN WAITING.` → `A MONK WHO WON'T TURN AROUND.` → `MY MIND ISN'T AT PEACE.`

segments.voice: First, the request. The Gateless Gate, a collection of Chan stories with short comments, tells this as one of its cases. Huike's words are simple enough for anyone to say at three in the morning: my mind is not at peace; please pacify it. Second, the answer. Bodhidharma doesn't offer advice or a technique. He says: bring me your mind, and I'll pacify it for you. Hand it over. Put it on the table. Third, the search. Huike looks. And he says: I've searched for my mind, and I can't find it. Bodhidharma answers: there, I have pacified it for you. That's the whole exchange. Chan remembers Huike as the student who received Bodhidharma's teaching, the second ancestor in its line. Fourth, what happened in that search. Huike was asked to do something odd: not to fix his mind, but to find it. When you go looking for the anxious mind, you find things: a thought about tomorrow, a tight feeling in the chest, a picture of someone's face, a sentence repeating itself. But they keep moving. You can't pick the whole thing up and hand it to anyone. Some readers hear Bodhidharma saying the trouble was never a solid object; others hear a teacher simply turning a student around to look. Either way, the peace in the story doesn't come from a new answer. It comes from looking straight at the question. When worry feels like a heavy thing to carry, this story offers a small experiment: go and find it.
screen: `MY MIND IS NOT AT PEACE.` · `BRING ME YOUR MIND.` · `I'VE SEARCHED AND CAN'T FIND IT.` · `LOOKING STRAIGHT AT THE WORRY.` · then, large: `I CAN'T FIND IT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look for your anxious mind. Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Bring up one small worry, not the biggest one. Let it be there. Now, gently, go looking for the mind that's worried. Where is it? In the head? The chest? Does it have a shape, an edge, a color? Each time you find a thought, notice it's already moving, and look again. No need to force an answer. If the worry softens, let it. If it doesn't, keep looking with curiosity. The bell holds the time.
Bring me your mind. Bodhidharma's answer to a student who asked for peace: not a fix, but an invitation to look. Today's word.
Your line: I can't find it. Today, when a worry shows up, pause and go looking for it, just for a breath or two. Day nine hundred thirteen.

914.title: The woodcutter
914.hook: Huineng, a poor woodcutter who can't read, hears the Diamond Sutra in the market and his mind opens
914.howItsDone: Chan and Zen communities honor Huineng as the Sixth Ancestor, and the Platform Sutra, his story and teaching, is read and taught in Chinese, Korean, Japanese and Vietnamese temples.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Huike went looking for his anxious mind. Your line: I can't find it. When you went looking for a worry, what did you find instead? Day nine hundred fourteen.

A young man in a market in the far south of China has just been paid for a load of firewood and turns toward the door. Near it, a stranger is reciting a Buddhist text out loud, just saying it, the way someone hums at work. The young man stops. He can't read. And as he listens, the Platform Sutra says, his mind opens. Today, the woodcutter Chan would come to honor as its Sixth Ancestor.
screen: `A STRANGER RECITING A SUTRA.` → `FIREWOOD SOLD IN THE MARKET.` → `THE WOODCUTTER STOPS.`

segments.voice: First, who he was. His name was Huineng, and the Platform Sutra lets him tell his own story. His father died when he was young. He and his mother were poor, and he sold firewood in the market to keep them both. He couldn't read or write. Second, what he heard. The text the stranger was reciting was the Diamond Sutra, a teaching on letting go of fixed ideas, even fixed ideas about the Buddha. Huineng asked where he had learned it. The man said: on East Mountain, from the teacher Hongren, who tells everyone to keep this sutra. The Platform Sutra says Huineng made sure his mother was provided for, and then walked north to find him. Third, the first meeting. Hongren asks where he's from and what he wants. Huineng says he's from the far south, and he wants only one thing: to become a Buddha. Hongren tests him with an insult. You're from the south, a barbarian, he says. How could you become a Buddha? Huineng answers: people may be from the north or the south, but Buddha-nature has no north or south. Fourth, the threshing room. Hongren doesn't praise him. He sends him to the back of the monastery to split wood and pound rice, and there Huineng works, unnoticed. Notice where this story puts its turning point: not in a temple hall or a library, but in a market, between a sale and the door, through a stranger who probably never knew. A line can arrive anywhere.
screen: `A WOODCUTTER WHO CAN'T READ.` · `THE DIAMOND SUTRA IN THE MARKET.` · `BUDDHA-NATURE HAS NO NORTH OR SOUTH.` · `SENT TO POUND RICE.` · then, large: `HEARD IN THE MARKET.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hear one line with fresh ears. Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Choose a sentence you've heard so often you've stopped hearing it: a saying from your family, a line from a prayer, a phrase from a song. Say it silently, slowly, as if a stranger in a market just said it and you were hearing it for the first time. Let one word stand out. Stay with that word for a few breaths. If nothing opens, that's fine; you've listened. The bell holds the time.
The woodcutter. Huineng, who couldn't read, heard the Diamond Sutra in a market and walked north to find the teacher. Today's word.
Your line: heard in the market. Today, listen for one sentence from a stranger, a sign or a passing conversation, and let it land. Day nine hundred fourteen.

915.title: Two verses on the wall
915.hook: the head monk writes that the mind is a mirror to be wiped; Huineng answers that there is no mirror stand
915.howItsDone: Chan and Zen students learn both verses, Shenxiu's and Huineng's, and teachers use them to talk about steady practice and the mind's original clarity.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the woodcutter Huineng heard a sutra between a sale and the door. Your line: heard in the market. What sentence did you hear with fresh ears? Day nine hundred fifteen.

Late at night, by lamplight, a monk walks down a corridor with a brush and ink. He writes a short verse on the wall and goes back to his room without signing it. In the morning the whole monastery is reading it. The teacher Hongren had set a test: write a verse that shows your understanding, and whoever truly understands will receive the robe and become the next teacher in the line. Everyone expected the head monk to win. This is his verse. Today, two verses on the wall.
screen: `A VERSE WRITTEN AT NIGHT.` → `HONGREN'S TEST.` → `TWO VERSES ON THE WALL.`

segments.voice: First, the mirror to be wiped. The head monk was Shenxiu, a respected teacher in his own right. His verse, in the Platform Sutra, says roughly this: the body is the tree of awakening, the mind is like a bright mirror on its stand; wipe it clean, again and again, and don't let dust gather. It's a beautiful picture of practice: steady, patient care. Second, a verse he can't write. In the threshing room, Huineng hears a boy chanting Shenxiu's lines. He can't read, so he asks someone to read the wall to him, and then asks someone to write his own answer beside it. Third, no tree, no stand. Huineng's verse turns Shenxiu's around: awakening has no tree, the bright mirror has no stand. Here the versions of the Platform Sutra differ. The older one found at Dunhuang says Buddha-nature is always clean and pure; later versions say that from the beginning there is not a single thing. Both end with the same question: where could the dust land? Fourth, what the two pictures mean. Shenxiu describes the mind as something to keep polishing. Huineng says the clear nature was never dirty in the first place. That night Hongren calls Huineng in secret, gives him the robe, and sends him south. Later Chan writers told the story as gradual against sudden, and it comes to us from Huineng's side. But both verses are still read, and some readers find room for both in practice: some wiping, and some moments of seeing there was nothing to wipe.
screen: `THE MIRROR TO BE WIPED.` · `A VERSE HE CAN'T WRITE.` · `NO TREE, NO STAND.` · `POLISHING, OR NOTHING TO POLISH.` · then, large: `WHERE DOES DUST LAND?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: wipe a mirror, then look. If there's a mirror nearby, or a phone screen, wipe it slowly with your sleeve or a cloth. Watch the smudges go. That's Shenxiu's verse: patient, honest work. Now set it down and close your eyes. Notice what's aware of the breath right now. Is there any dust on that? Any smudge? Rest for a few breaths with Huineng's question, where does dust land, without needing an answer. Then let both pictures go and simply breathe. The bell holds the time.
Two verses on the wall. Shenxiu's mirror to be wiped, and Huineng's answer: no stand, and nowhere for dust to land. Today's word.
screen: `TWO VERSES ON THE WALL — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: where does dust land. Today, when you wipe a counter or a screen, ask the question once. Day nine hundred fifteen.

916.title: The Chan monastery
916.hook: Mazu and Baizhang: work, meals and meditation shaped into one life
916.howItsDone: In Chan and Zen monasteries today, residents share daily work periods, often called samu in Japanese, alongside meditation and meals eaten together in a set form.

segments.voice: Yesterday, two verses on the wall: a mirror to be wiped, and a mirror with no stand. Your line: where does dust land. Did you ask it while wiping something? Day nine hundred sixteen.

A wooden board is struck outside the meditation hall, and the monks file out. Not to chant this time. To the fields. They carry hoes and baskets. The cook is already at the stove, the youngest monks are hauling water, and somewhere among them, bent over a row of vegetables, is the abbot. In a Chan monastery, the stories say, nobody was too senior to dig. Two teachers stand behind this picture: Mazu, who shook his students awake, and his student Baizhang, who gave the community its shape. Today, the Chan monastery.
screen: `THE BOARD IS STRUCK.` → `EVERYONE TO THE FIELDS.` → `THE ABBOT DIGS TOO.`

segments.voice: First, Mazu. He was a teacher in Huineng's line, remembered for blunt answers, shouts and sudden questions. In the Gateless Gate, a monk asks him what Buddha is, and Mazu answers: this very mind is Buddha. Not somewhere else, not later. This mind, the one asking. Second, Baizhang and the rules. Chan is remembered as a school of meditation, and you might expect a Chan monastery to do nothing but sit. Tradition credits Baizhang with shaping rules for Chan communities, and those rules put sitting inside a whole day: a hall for meditation, meals eaten together in order and in quiet, and shared work for everyone. Third, work, meals and sitting as one life. In that picture, digging the garden isn't time off from practice, and washing the bowls isn't a chore to rush through. The same attention that watches the breath in the hall watches the hoe in the soil. Fourth, water and firewood. A layman named Pang, who studied with Mazu, put it in a short verse. His supernatural powers and marvelous deeds, he said, were these: carrying water and hauling firewood. It's a joke, and it isn't. If this very mind is Buddha, as Mazu said, then it's this mind that carries the water. A modern day has its own version of Baizhang's fields: dishes, laundry, commuting, typing. The Chan monastery's claim is that none of it has to be wasted time.
screen: `MAZU: THIS VERY MIND IS BUDDHA.` · `BAIZHANG: RULES FOR A WHOLE DAY.` · `WORK, MEALS AND SITTING AS ONE LIFE.` · `CARRYING WATER, HAULING FIREWOOD.` · then, large: `WORK IS PRACTICE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do one chore as practice. Choose a chore you'll do today: dishes, folding clothes, sweeping, making a bed. Now, sitting here, walk through it slowly in your mind. Feel the water's temperature, the weight of the cloth, the sound of the broom. Notice where the mind usually runs off to while you do it. Then decide, gently, that this time you'll stay with your hands. Come back to the breath, and let the chore wait for its moment. The bell holds the time.
The Chan monastery. Mazu's this very mind is Buddha, and Baizhang's day of sitting, meals and shared work, everyone in the fields together. Today's word.
Your line: work is practice. Today, do that one chore with your whole attention, start to finish, and see how it feels. Day nine hundred sixteen.

917.title: The persecution of 845
917.hook: a Tang emperor closes the monasteries; the teachings that needed little come through
917.howItsDone: Chinese Buddhists remember the persecution under Emperor Wuzong as one of the hard turns in their history, and Chan and Pure Land communities often tell it as part of their own story of carrying the teaching through.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Chan monastery, where Mazu and Baizhang shaped work, meals and sitting into one life. Your line was work is practice. Which chore did you turn into practice? Day nine hundred seventeen.

Bells are being lowered from temple towers and carted off to be melted down. Bronze images go into the furnaces after them. Monks and nuns are told to take off their robes and go home as ordinary subjects. The halls are emptied, the gates are shut. This is China under the Tang emperor Wuzong, and a monk from Japan, far from home, is watching it happen and writing it down in his diary, while he tries to get himself and his books out of the country. Today, the persecution of 845, and the question it leaves on the table: when the buildings go, what's left?
screen: `BELLS GO TO THE FURNACE.` → `ROBES COME OFF.` → `WHAT'S LEFT?`

segments.voice: First, the orders. The official histories of the Tang dynasty date the harshest of Emperor Wuzong's decrees to 845. The court had come to see the monasteries as a drain: land, metal and people outside the tax rolls, serving a teaching that came from abroad. Wuzong himself favored Daoist masters. His decrees closed monasteries across the empire and sent monks and nuns back to lay life. Second, the eyewitness. The monk from Japan was Ennin, and his diary of his years in China lets us see it from the road: monks forced into lay clothes, images stripped, foreign monks sent away. To get home, he put on ordinary clothes himself. Third, what came through. The worst of it was short; the histories tell that Wuzong died soon after, and the next emperor eased the ban. But schools that leaned on great libraries, rich estates and the court's favor were badly shaken. A common way of telling the story is that two schools came through more easily. Chan, whose monks, like Baizhang's, worked their own fields and taught face to face. And Pure Land, whose practice could be carried in a single breath: the name of Amitabha Buddha, said by anyone, anywhere, with no building at all. Fourth, the old teaching underneath. The Buddha taught that all conditioned things pass away. An empire can take bells, roofs and robes. It is much harder to confiscate a habit of sitting still, or a name a grandmother says over the stove. That closes a week that began with Bodhidharma facing a wall, a week of stories saying the teaching did not live in the buildings.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor something that survived. Settle, and let the breath find its own pace. Bring to mind one thing that came through a hard time and reached you: a recipe in someone's handwriting, a song a parent sang, an old building on your street, a habit you kept through a bad year. Hold it in your attention. Notice what it needed in order to last, and what it turned out not to need. If you'd like, bow to it slightly, with your head or only in your mind. The bell holds the time.
The persecution of 845. The year, as the Tang histories date it, when an emperor closed the monasteries, and the teaching went on in fields, kitchens and a spoken name. Today's word.
Your line: what survived. Today, when you pass something old, a tree, a wall, a worn tool, stop for one breath and wonder what it came through. That's the week. Day nine hundred seventeen.
